articles.title: Should I buy a Rumawip or other affordable housing unit?
articles.excerpt: Tens of thousands of affordable homes sit unsold while city prices hit records. Sean explains who these schemes really serve, and how they change the price of the homes around them.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is an affordable housing unit a good buy, and how do these schemes affect other buyers?
articles.answer: If you qualify and the location suits you, it can be very good value, because these homes are heavily subsidised. But Sean says the schemes have produced unsold homes while their cost is passed on to the open-market homes around them.
points: A good location makes it a bargain
The income limit is high
Open-market buyers pay for it
Compare it with open-market homes

articles.title: Landed or condo: which holds its value better?
articles.excerpt: A reader assumes landed homes are guaranteed to appreciate while condos age. Sean explains why that view is hindsight, where condos win, and the price ceiling open landed homes run into.
articles.viewerQuestion: In a sought-after area such as Bukit Jalil, Hartamas or PJ, how would a condo's value hold up against a landed home over the long run?
articles.answer: Landed terrace houses do appreciate fastest, but "guaranteed" is hindsight. Condos in good locations grow a little more slowly yet earn far more rent, and older landed homes without security face a ceiling on what buyers will pay.
points: Landed wins on growth, condos win on rent
Yesterday's safe bet was once the fringe
Open landed homes hit a price ceiling
Big landed homes are hard to sell
questions: Do landed homes always appreciate more than condos?
Which is better for rental income: condo or landed?
Why do older landed homes without security have a price ceiling?
Are large landed homes hard to sell in Malaysia?
Should I buy a condo for rental yield or a landed home for capital growth?

articles.title: Should I buy now the condo I'll downsize to in 20 years?
articles.excerpt: A 36-year-old father of three wants a Bukit Jalil condo to rent out now and retire into later, but it needs RM150,000 down. Sean says no: sell the old apartment, regain two 90% loans and buy for cash flow.
articles.viewerQuestion: Does it make sense to buy now, rent it out even at a small loss, and move in at retirement? Or should he sell the Shah Alam apartment?
articles.answer: Don't buy it. Nobody knows what he will need, earn or be able to do at 56, and putting RM150,000 into a 70% loan for an own-stay project is the wrong tool. Sell the apartment, which frees a 90% loan for each of them, and buy for cash flow instead.
points: Twenty years is too far to plan a home
Joint names used up both 90% loans
At 70%, many units beat this one
The apartment is ready to sell

articles.title: Is buying an auction property worth the risk?
articles.excerpt: Auction prices can be the market's most genuine, but your deposit is lost if financing fails. Sean explains how auctions work and what to check before you bid.
articles.viewerQuestion: How does buying at auction work, and should a first-time buyer try it?
articles.answer: It can be a genuine bargain, but only for buyers with capital and knowledge. You pay 10% to bid and must settle the rest within 90 to 120 days, on a loan based on your winning price, so first-time buyers without savings are better off with new properties.
points: The loan follows the price you pay
Some deals can't be financed
You buy it as it is
Prices fall each round without bids

articles.title: Should I buy a property with my boyfriend or girlfriend?
articles.excerpt: Couples who buy in joint names find a break-up leaves both of them on the loan. Sean explains why he discourages it, and the arrangement he prefers.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should an unmarried couple buy a property together in joint names?
articles.answer: No. Joint names use up both partners' 90% loans on one property, and nobody plans for a break-up. If you must, set the terms out in writing; better still, buy in one name with the other as guarantor.
points: It wastes your 90% loans
Break-ups don't service loans
Joining names often means overreaching
One name, one guarantor

articles.title: I cancelled my booking. Was it FOMO, or the right call?
articles.excerpt: A 25-year-old booked a RM640,000 unit on a promised 15% return, then cancelled. Sean explains why that was right, and how to tell what you can actually afford.
articles.viewerQuestion: Was walking away right, or too conservative? And how does he stop worrying that prices will run away before he is ready?
articles.answer: Cancelling was right. The numbers only worked if nothing went wrong, and on his income a property of around RM300,000 to RM400,000 is the safer place to start.
points: A 15% return is a red flag
Student-style buildings are hard to exit
He could not survive a bad year
Time yourself, not the market
questions: Did I make a mistake cancelling my property booking?
How much property can I afford on my income?
Is it safe to buy a property with a 15% promised return?
What should I check before paying a booking fee?
How do I compare property prices per square foot across areas?

articles.title: I own four cars and want a fifth. Should I buy property instead?
articles.excerpt: A 28-year-old in Kuching with RM500,000 in fixed deposits, four cars and a baby on the way asks about landed homes, his rented-out house and his uncle's. Sean says fix the spending first.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should he keep his rented house, buy his uncle's, and choose landed or an apartment for his family home, and how much should he put down?
articles.answer: Keep the house he owns and, for a family with this many cars, a landed home makes sense. But on RM8,000 with RM6,800 spent each month, the real problem is spending: until he controls it and stops buying cars, the property questions don't matter.
points: His rented house is earning its keep
His uncle's house depends on the price
Cars lose value; homes gain it
Count cash flow, not units

articles.title: Is a cheap unit with good rent worth buying?
articles.excerpt: A buyer is offered two old units in central KL at RM160,000 each, renting to foreign workers at a 6.33% yield. Sean explains why cheap is not the same as money-making.
articles.viewerQuestion: With steady rent but little prospect of the price rising, is it still a good investment?
articles.answer: No. The cash flow works, but with almost no capital appreciation, a loan slot used up and only about RM200 a month to show for it, Sean says better deals are available and this one is not worth the headspace.
points: The yield clears the bar, just
There is almost nothing to sell later
It spends a 90% loan slot
Better deals are out there

articles.title: When should you stop renting and buy a home?
articles.excerpt: A 34-year-old renter is tired of moving and wants a home of his own, but friends warn him off. Sean tests the decision with his 85% rule.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should he buy a home in the area he already lives in, or keep renting and invest the money instead?
articles.answer: Buy it. He can afford it, he knows the area, and the unit would rent for most of its instalment if his plans ever change. That is what makes an own-stay purchase safe.
points: It passes the 85% rule
He is buying where he already lives
His foundations are in place
A home pays you in certainty
questions: When should I stop renting and buy my own home?
How do I know if I can afford to buy a house?
What is the 85% rule for buying a home?
Should I buy a home in the area I already live in?
Is it better to buy a home or keep renting and invest?

articles.title: What should you check when you get your keys?
articles.excerpt: Most buyers hunt for scratches and hollow tiles and miss what stops a home from working. Sean sets out what to check first in a defect inspection.
articles.viewerQuestion: What should you check during a defect inspection, and in what order?
articles.answer: Check function before looks. Test every power point, water point, door and window first, compare the unit against your sale agreement, then move on to cosmetic flaws, and report everything through the proper channel.
points: Utilities come first
Water problems hide
Your sale agreement is the checklist
Hollow tiles are more serious than they look
questions: What should I check first during a defect inspection?
How do I test if tiles are hollow?
What should I bring for a defect inspection?
How long is the defect liability period?
Can I claim for leaks after moving in?

articles.title: I bought at a discount. Why am I still losing money?
articles.excerpt: A homeowner who bought "at a good rate" during COVID now struggles with the instalment and cannot find tenants. Sean explains why a discount is not a bargain, and how to decide whether to hold, rent or sell.
articles.viewerQuestion: Did he buy into a money-losing development, and what should he do now?
articles.answer: A discount only helps if the price ends up below the area's median, not just below the project's old price. For a home already bought, the question now is whether to hold, rent or sell, and that depends on valuation, recent sales and the loan balance.
points: The discount was measured against the wrong number
A quiet address does not draw tenants
The 85% test was never done
Who loses depends on when they bought
questions: Why does buying a property at a discount still lose money?
How do I know if my condo can cover its own instalment with rent?
Should I hold, rent out or sell my property that is not renting?
How do I check if my property is really worth what I paid?
Why can't I find tenants for my condo even at lower rent?

articles.title: I'm between jobs with savings. Should I buy my first property now?
articles.excerpt: A 27-year-old who left medicine for a master's degree has about RM380,000 saved and wants a RM400,000 investment unit in the Klang Valley, which he barely knows. Sean says research now, buy after six months in a new job.
articles.viewerQuestion: How should he choose between projects in unfamiliar areas, do view and floor level matter, and what should he do with his cash?
articles.answer: Wait. Without a payslip he can't qualify for a loan anyway, and a 35-year commitment needs a steady income first. Use the time to get to know the Klang Valley, then buy once he has six months of income from his new job.
points: Invest where people move for work
View matters only at the extremes
Completed units let you roll faster
His cash is well placed

articles.title: Should I spend most of my cash on a fifth property before I marry?
articles.excerpt: A 27-year-old commission earner with four properties wants to put RM214,000 of his RM300,000 savings into a dual-key unit yielding 7.3%, a year before his wedding. Sean says the deal is fine; the timing isn't.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is this purchase a good move given his commitments and wedding plans, and is spending RM214,000 the smartest route to passive income?
articles.answer: No, not now. The property itself is a solid buy, but with renovation it would take about RM260,000 of his RM300,000, leaving a few months of spending on a commission income just before a wedding. Rushing because he doubts next year's income shows he isn't ready.
points: Cash flow is what sinks investors
Paying more cash isn't smarter
Doubting your income means you're not ready
Low valuations are normal in new projects

articles.title: Must your first property also be your home?
articles.excerpt: A 26-year-old bought an investment condo before a family home, and his future in-laws disapprove. Sean explains why investing first can be the smarter order.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is it better to buy a home first and invest later? And how should he explain his plan to in-laws who think he is being too aggressive?
articles.answer: Invest first and keep renting your home. Use your strongest borrowing years and your cheapest loans on property that tenants help pay for, and buy the family home later.
points: The 90% loans are worth using early
A home tends to become a big commitment
Judge it over 20 years, not in month one
Renting keeps the couple flexible
questions: Should I buy an investment property before my own home?
How do I explain to my in-laws that renting and investing is a good plan?
What are the benefits of using a 90% loan for an investment property?
How long should I wait before buying my next investment property?
Should a young couple rent their home and invest first?

articles.title: Is it worth paying to furnish a unit before renting it out?
articles.excerpt: Spending RM30,000 to furnish a unit for RM500 more rent looks like a five-year payback. Sean explains how he weighs the cost, and why higher rent can add to a property's value.
articles.viewerQuestion: How do you decide whether furnishing a rental unit is worth the cost?
articles.answer: Furnish to let the unit faster or at a higher rent, but compare the right numbers. Against the roughly RM12,000 a unit needs anyway to be livable, a RM30,000 package costs about RM18,000 more, which buys time and design sense, and higher rent can lift what the property is worth.
points: Compare against the bare minimum
You are paying for time and design sense
Rent can lift the property's value
First impressions win tenants

articles.title: Is a guaranteed rental return worth buying into?
articles.excerpt: A reader has booked a hotel unit with a guaranteed 7% return. Sean explains where the guarantee really comes from, and why the exit is the bigger problem.
articles.viewerQuestion: He worries about the narrow access road, the operator choosing not to renew after nine years, and another pandemic. Is this kind of investment worth it?
articles.answer: Stay away unless it is a third or fourth property you can afford to lose. The guaranteed return is your own borrowed money paid back to you, the price is inflated, and the hotel operator is your only way out.
points: The guarantee is built into the price
You are paying city-centre prices for Genting
There is only one way out
The real return is thinner than 7%
questions: Is a guaranteed rental return worth buying into?
How does a guaranteed rental return scheme work?
What happens if the hotel operator leaves?
Is a hotel unit a good investment?
How to evaluate a property with guaranteed yield?

articles.title: What does buying a property really cost beyond the 10%?
articles.excerpt: Most first-time buyers budget the deposit and nothing else. Sean lists the costs that kept surprising him on his first purchase.
articles.viewerQuestion: What else do you actually have to pay when you buy a property?
articles.answer: Budget well beyond the deposit. Legal fees on both the purchase and the loan, transfer stamp duty, valuation, handover deposits, compulsory insurance and yearly taxes all fall on the buyer, and a subsale costs the most upfront.
points: Legal fees come with more than one agreement
The transfer duty is the big one
Handover comes with deposits
Some costs never stop
questions: What are the hidden costs of buying a property in Malaysia beyond the 10% deposit?
How much stamp duty do I need to pay when buying a house?
What legal fees are involved in a property purchase?
What deposits do I need to pay before getting the keys?
What ongoing costs should I budget for after buying a property?

articles.title: I earn well but fear losing my savings. Should I invest in property?
articles.excerpt: A 30-year-old in Melaka earning RM24,000 a month, with RM450,000 in cash, fears one wrong move. Sean says buy a rental unit well within her means, and leave renovate-and-flip alone.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is she ready to invest in property, what should she buy, and should she flip houses or start a business instead?
articles.answer: Yes, she is ready, but should play well within her means: a rental unit of RM500,000 to RM1 million in a proven KL location, where the rent covers the instalment. Buying an old house to renovate and sell is where people without construction experience lose money.
points: A rental unit has few unknowns
She can absorb a bad month
The contractor wins most flips
Melaka's high-rise market is weak

articles.title: Why hold a property for 35 years instead of selling it?
articles.excerpt: A first-time buyer plans to sell after five years for a RM100,000 gain and asks why anyone would hold for 35. Sean explains the long equity game and why cash loses to inflation.
articles.viewerQuestion: What is the point of holding several properties for 30 to 35 years if they may be hard to rent or sell by then?
articles.answer: Flipping is hard now because developers already price in the gains, so Sean holds properties whose rent covers the instalment on zero down payment and lets tenants pay them off. Cash from a sale loses value to inflation while the property keeps pace, though there is no rule that you must hold to the end.
points: Each RM500 surplus is about RM100,000 of value
Cash loses to inflation
Older units still rent
Tenants and the bank do the work

articles.title: Can I buy a terrace house and run my tuition class in it?
articles.excerpt: A teacher in Kuantan wants a RM440,000 double-storey house to hold tuition classes downstairs and rent out the rooms upstairs. Sean says check first whether it can legally host a business.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should he buy the house to run his tuition class downstairs and rent out the rooms upstairs?
articles.answer: Only once he knows he can legally run a tuition centre there. Many do it in houses, but a residential title isn't meant for it, and neighbours, safety and licensing can end the plan. Without the business, the house has to stand as an investment, and its rent won't cover the instalment.
points: A home is not a licensed premises
Neighbours bear the cost
Landed rent rarely covers the loan
Rooms for transferred staff can pay

articles.title: How much housing loan can I actually get?
articles.excerpt: Banks decide with one number, your debt service ratio. Rena Choong shows how to estimate your own loan eligibility before visiting a sales gallery, and what CCRIS and CTOS reveal.
articles.viewerQuestion: How do banks decide how much housing loan you can get, and how can you work it out yourself before you start looking?
articles.answer: Banks use your debt service ratio: all your loan repayments, existing and new, divided by your net income. Work out your own figure first, so you only look at properties you can finance and don't collect rejections.
points: The DSR limit rises with income
A quick formula gives your limit
Your repayment record sets your rate
Card balances count, not card limits
questions: How do banks calculate how much housing loan I can get?
What is a debt service ratio and how do I calculate it?
How does CCRIS affect my housing loan application?
How can I check my loan eligibility before buying a house?
What can I do to improve my chances of getting a housing loan approved?

articles.title: Flexi, semi-flexi or fixed: how does housing loan interest work?
articles.excerpt: Most buyers compare loans only by the monthly instalment. Rena Choong explains how housing loans charge interest, why a lump sum belongs there, and when full flexi is worth its fee.
articles.viewerQuestion: How does a housing loan charge interest compared with a personal or car loan, and which type should you take if you want to pay it down faster?
articles.answer: A housing loan charges interest only on what you still owe, so a lump-sum prepayment cuts the interest and can shorten the loan, while personal and car loans fix the interest up front. If you will prepay or draw money back often, take a full flexi loan; on a semi-flexi loan you must ask the bank to apply any extra payment to the principal.
points: Flat-rate loans charge all interest up front
Housing loan interest falls as you pay
Extra money in semi-flexi just sits there
Full flexi works like a cheaper overdraft

What is the difference between full flexi and semi-flexi housing loans?
How can I pay off my housing loan faster?

articles.title: Why was my housing loan rejected?
articles.excerpt: A rejected loan stays on record and makes the next bank wary. Rena Choong goes through the most common reasons banks say no, and what to fix before you apply again.
articles.viewerQuestion: What are the most common reasons banks reject a housing loan, and how do you avoid them?
articles.answer: Most rejections are predictable: a DSR over the limit, recent arrears in CCRIS, a restructured loan, or a legal or AKPK record. Fix what you can and wait for a clean record before applying, because each rejection is visible to the next bank.
points: Recent arrears mean an upfront no
Restructuring is worse than refinancing
Legal records block even eligible buyers
Every application leaves a mark

articles.title: My mother gave me her old house. Should I sell it?
articles.excerpt: A 53-year-old was gifted the Penang semi-D his mother bought 40 years ago. It barely rents, but he is attached to it. Sean says to find its true value first, then decide what the money is for.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should he sell the house, given its low rent, or keep it for its sentimental value and as his only landed property?
articles.answer: Either is defensible, because he has no urgent need for the money. First find out what the house is really worth. If a buyer offers above market value, Sean would sell, clear any housing loan and set up his child's education fund; otherwise holding it is fine.
points: Rent is the wrong yardstick
Sentiment has a cost
Sell when you don't need the money
Without a goal, nothing moves

articles.title: I'm over 60. Should I still invest in property?
articles.excerpt: A reader over 60 is being offered short-stay units promising 9% returns. Sean explains why property loses its main advantage at that age, and what to consider instead.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should she invest in property at her age? Should she pay cash or borrow, buy new or subsale, and are these short-stay projects worth it?
articles.answer: Probably not as a main plan. Property's big advantage is decades of cheap borrowing that tenants help repay, and at 60 that is mostly gone. Low-risk options paying a similar return, without the hassle or locked-up money, suit her better.
points: The leverage advantage is mostly gone
Property locks your money up
Other assets pay similar returns more easily
Advertised short-stay returns rarely last

Can I still get a housing loan at 60?
Are short stay units with high returns a good investment?
Should I pay cash or take a loan for an investment property?
How do property returns compare with fixed deposits and EPF?

articles.title: My ex and I own a house together. Should we sell or rent it out?
articles.excerpt: A couple bought a Puncak Alam home in joint names, then broke up badly. Selling now costs him about RM16,000; she wants to rent it out for five years. Sean says take the loss and move on.
articles.viewerQuestion: From an investment point of view, is selling now the right choice?
articles.answer: Sell. Holding might work out better on paper, but not for him: two people who can't talk will fight over tenants and costs for years. About RM16,000 is a fair price for a clean slate, even if he pays her share as a farewell gift.
points: Numbers won't settle a feud
He made the choices
Discounts were money from the future
Unfurnished units rent cheaply

articles.title: Is a leasehold condo with 60-odd years left too risky to buy?
articles.excerpt: A couple love a leasehold condo but worry it will be hard to sell with 60 to 70 years left on the lease. Sean says the lease is the smaller risk; buying together unmarried is the bigger one.
articles.viewerQuestion: Will a condo with 60 to 70 years left on its lease be hard to sell, even at the price they paid?
articles.answer: The lease isn't the real risk. If the rent covers the instalment, they can always rent the unit out and wait, so they can buy if they like it. What worries Sean is buying jointly without an agreement.
points: Lease renewals can lift prices
Freehold isn't absolute either
The real exit risk is financing
Here the rent covers the loan

articles.title: Salaried, on commission or self-employed: what trips up a loan?
articles.excerpt: Banks judge your income by how you earn it. Rena Choong explains where employees, commission earners and business owners go wrong, and which records to prepare months ahead.
articles.viewerQuestion: What mistakes get housing loans rejected for employees, commission earners and the self-employed, and how should each prepare?
articles.answer: Know which income group you are in, because each is judged on different records: payslips and EPF for employees, commission statements and tax returns for agents, and company accounts and bank statements for business owners. Prepare them months before you buy, and never dress your income up.
points: Employees: the documents must match
Bonuses count for less than basic pay
Commission earners need tax returns
Business owners are judged by the company

articles.title: Is "location, location, location" still the rule?
articles.excerpt: A young investor has shortlisted Bangsar South by its rental demand. Sean argues that location is not what makes you money; the price you pay against the area median is.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is "location, location, location" still the rule? Should he pay more for a newer project or buy an older subsale, and could he fund it with a 36-month interest-free credit card plan?
articles.answer: Location matters less than people think. Most KL areas will end up with the same amenities, so your profit is decided by your entry price: buy below the area's median price.

High rent follows temporary demand
New costs more but ages better
A subsale starts earning sooner

articles.title: I'm a civil servant. How should I use my LPPSA housing loan?
articles.excerpt: Civil servants can borrow from LPPSA on top of the usual bank loans. Rena Choong explains why the order you use them in matters, and the catches in LPPSA's terms.
articles.viewerQuestion: How does an LPPSA loan differ from a bank loan, and when should a civil servant use it?
articles.answer: Use your two 90% bank loans first and keep LPPSA, which can finance 100%, for the third property. LPPSA repayments come off your payslip, so using it first lowers the net income banks see and leaves your next bank loan at 70%.
points: The order changes your margins
A fixed 4% over a very long term
Full instalments start after two years
LPPSA has its own limits

articles.title: My unit has no strata title yet. Does it matter?
articles.excerpt: A high-rise unit still under the master title can be harder to sell and finance. Sean explains what a strata title proves, and what to ask about parcels and share units.
articles.viewerQuestion: What does it mean when a unit is still under the master title, and can it still be sold?
articles.answer: It means you can't yet prove ownership of your own unit. You can still sell it, but only with the consent of the land owner, usually the developer, which adds a hurdle for buyers and banks. A strata title removes it.
points: The title is the unit's birth certificate
A missing title may be delay or bad news
Ownership gives you a vote
Parcels decide what you pay for

articles.title: A baby is coming. Move in, or rent out our first home?
articles.excerpt: A couple bought a new condo as their first home, but their first child arrives as it is handed over. Sean explains why he would rent it out and stay with family for now.
articles.viewerQuestion: With a baby coming, should they stay with his parents, rent the unit out and live elsewhere, or move in as planned despite the renovation noise from 1,300 new neighbours?
articles.answer: Stay with family for the first year or two and rent River Park out from handover. Treat it as an investment, and move somewhere that suits the baby later, renting if you need to.
points: A newborn needs hands more than space
The unit works better as a rental
1,300 new units is less of a threat than it looks

articles.title: Should you buy new from a developer or a subsale?
articles.excerpt: A new launch and a subsale unit can cost the same on paper but ask for very different cash, time and risk. Sean explains who each one suits.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should you buy new from a developer, or a subsale unit?
articles.answer: It depends on your cash and experience. Investors with capital should favour a subsale, where you can see the real condition and rent from day one. First-time buyers short on cash are better served by a new launch.

articles.title: Can I really buy a property with no money down?
articles.excerpt: Discounts, rebates and cash backs promise a property with no capital. Sean explains how these deals work, and why you still need cash and a strong loan profile to use them.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is a no money down deal really free of money, and who can use one?
articles.answer: Only by the end of the deal. You still need cash to get it started and the income to qualify for a loan at the right margin; the "zero" appears only once the bank releases the loan and refunds what you paid.

articles.title: Is an older Bukit Jalil apartment a good first investment?
articles.excerpt: A 33-year-old with savings and no debts wants a well-kept 1990s subsale unit in Bukit Jalil whose rent already covers the loan. Sean calls it safe, but would look for better options first.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is this subsale unit a good first investment property?
articles.answer: It is a very safe deal she can afford, and she wouldn't lose money. But Sean wouldn't buy it himself, because the same budget can buy newer units with more room to grow. With no rush, she should negotiate harder and compare all four buying channels first.
points: The rent already covers the loan
Old buildings protect the bottom, not the upside
Subsale takes real cash
The location is strong

articles.title: Cheap old house or new house with no down payment?
articles.excerpt: An unmarried couple must choose between a cheap 30-year-old house needing renovation and a new one with a bigger instalment. Sean says the real question is whose income the loan depends on.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should they spend most of their savings on the old house with the easy instalment, or take the new house with little cash upfront but double the monthly commitment?
articles.answer: Take the old house, and buy it in one name. On one income, a RM3,000 instalment is out of reach, and counting on a partner who has not committed to living in Seremban is the real risk.
points: Do not borrow on income you cannot count on
Compare with the area median, not the new house
Renovation does not add its cost to the value
An old house is as good as how it was lived in
questions: Should I buy an old house that needs renovation or a new house with no down payment?
Should an unmarried couple buy a house in joint names?
How much renovation cost should I budget for an old house?
Is it safe to take a bigger loan based on my partner's income?
How do I check if an old house is priced fairly?

articles.title: Should I buy my own place, or wait until I can afford it?
articles.excerpt: A 34-year-old in oil and gas earns RM11,000 but has only months of savings and likes a new PJ project costing RM3,000 a month. Sean says it is that unit she cannot afford, not property.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should she buy that unit for own stay or investment, keep renting, or do something else?
articles.answer: Not now. Her income qualifies for a loan, but what is left each month cannot carry a RM3,000 commitment. Stay put, build savings and income, and when ready, buy a cheaper unit for investment first while she still values flexibility.
points: It's that unit she can't afford
Savings are the real issue
The RM1,500 is cheap rent
Single means flexible

articles.title: I'm in my 70s. What should my daughter do with our paid-off house?
articles.excerpt: A mother in her 70s has mapped out what her daughter should do with their landed home after she passes. Sean explains why cash and careful plans may not serve the next generation.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is it sensible for the daughter, after her mother has passed away, to rent out the house for about RM3,000, buy a RM300,000 to RM350,000 condo near work, and do her own repairs to save money?
articles.answer: Sean wouldn't lock the daughter into a plan. She could simply keep living in the house, and should first work out what she wants; if she does invest, a loan works better than cash, and she should buy as soon as a unit's rent covers its instalment rather than wait.
points: Cash loses value faster than it seems
Property bought in cash is a weak investment
Property pays when you borrow
Let the next generation choose
questions: Should I rent out my paid-off house and buy a cheaper condo?
Is it better to invest in property with cash or a loan?
How much emergency fund should I keep before investing?
Should I refinance my paid-off house to invest?
How do I decide between keeping a house or investing for my children?

articles.title: Should parents buy property for their children?
articles.excerpt: Some parents pay the down payment on their children's homes; some children ask for their parents' EPF. Sean explains when help teaches responsibility, and when it breeds entitlement.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should parents buy property for their children, and should children ask them to?
articles.answer: Parents can help, but use it to teach: pay the down payment and let the child pay the instalments, as savings for the future. Children should stand on their own feet; borrowing a sum and repaying it is fine, but asking for parents' savings to invest is not.
points: Paying the instalment teaches responsibility
Handouts breed entitlement
Parents' savings aren't yours to risk
Know what a home costs to carry

articles.title: My parents will pay half. Must I buy a home to live in?
articles.excerpt: A first-time investor's parents will pay half the price, but only for a home to live in. Sean explains how to protect a one-income household and handle the condition.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is her money enough, or too risky while her husband's business is unstable? Should she buy new or subsale, and how should she handle her parents' condition?
articles.answer: Protect your savings while the household runs on one income, and accept your parents' help graciously. Buy through a channel that needs little cash, and if the condition is a home, choose one that would still rent well.
points: Her savings are the household's safety net
Subsale and auction need too much cash
New launches and bulk deals need the least cash
Half the price is generous, with strings
questions: How much savings should I keep before buying a house?
Which way of buying needs the least cash upfront?
Should first-time buyers avoid auction properties?
How do I handle parents who want to help buy a house?
Can I afford a house on a single income?

articles.title: Our family bought units through a property guru. How do we get out?
articles.excerpt: A viewer's parents bought several units through a property guru at the 2018 peak and now pay thousands a month to hold them. Sean explains how the scheme worked and how to decide what to sell.
articles.viewerQuestion: How deep is the trouble, and what can the family do when selling most of the units means taking a loss?
articles.answer: Bad, but recoverable. Put every unit into one table to see which can be sold and which must be held, and ask her father to refinance the family house for a standby credit line instead of selling it.
points: The cash back was never spare money
Compressed loans hid the real risk
A table shows which units to release
Without cover, debt passes to the family
questions: How do I decide which property units to sell and which to hold?
What is a compressed loan and why is it risky?
What happens to my housing loan if I die without MRTA?
Should I sell my fully paid house or refinance it for cash?
How do I rent out my unit and cover the monthly shortfall?

articles.title: How do you know a project is not overpriced?
articles.excerpt: Projects borrow the name of a famous neighbourhood to charge its prices. Sean walks through the research that shows what an address is really worth.
articles.viewerQuestion: What research do you need to do to know whether a project is priced right?
articles.answer: Go beyond the listing. Work out where the real neighbourhood ends, which tier of tenant it attracts, and compare the project only against like-for-like transacted prices: new against new, old against old, in the same tier.
points: A borrowed name does not bring borrowed rents
Know which tier you are buying into
Compare new with new and old with old
Make sure two rental plans break even
questions: How do I know if a property project is overpriced?
What research should I do before buying a property?
How do I compare property prices in the same area?
What is the difference between tier 1, tier 2, and tier 3 areas?
How can I check if a property's rental income covers the mortgage?

articles.title: Which taxes do I pay when I own and sell property?
articles.excerpt: Beyond the price, owners pay stamp duty, assessment, quit rent and RPGT, and income tax decides whether you can borrow at all. Sean goes through the five.
articles.viewerQuestion: Which taxes should a property buyer in Malaysia budget for?
articles.answer: Five: stamp duty when you buy, assessment and quit rent every year you own it, RPGT when you sell at a gain, and income tax. For a young buyer, income tax matters first, because a declared income is the proof a bank lends on.
points: Declared income is what banks lend on
Stamp duty comes twice, in cash
Two taxes recur every year
Selling has its own rules

articles.title: When does refinancing my housing loan make sense?
articles.excerpt: Refinancing can lower your rate, release equity, win back a 90% loan or clear expensive debt. Rena Choong explains each use, and the valuation and income tests that decide whether yours works.
articles.viewerQuestion: What can refinancing a housing loan achieve, and how do you know whether yours qualifies?
articles.answer: Refinance only with a clear purpose: a lower rate, cash from equity you have built, a 90% loan quota back, or clearing high-interest debt. Whether it works depends on the bank's valuation and your income today. If you pay around 4.5% and a bank covers the switching costs, Rena calls it a no-brainer.
points: Refinancing lends 80%, not 90%
Cashing out has its own income test
A small rate cut adds up
Consolidate bad debt, never restructure

articles.title: Can a rent-to-rent deal help me build a portfolio fast?
articles.excerpt: A 26-year-old earning about RM3,000 plans to use an agency's rent-to-rent guarantee to buy two units within a year. Sean explains why the plan, not the property, is the problem.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should he use the rent-to-rent guarantee on a completed unit now, so its rent helps him buy a second property within six to 12 months?
articles.answer: No. Sean's problem is not the project or the scheme but the rush: on a RM3,000 income he is not ready to carry one property, let alone two, and a guarantee does not make an investment safe.
points: Guarantees sell to fear and laziness
The contract decides everything
One unit already takes half his income
The guarantee is priced in

articles.title: We'll retire with six properties. What should we sell, and when?
articles.excerpt: A couple of 50 and 54 plan to retire in 2032, sell their shop lot and landed home, pay off two apartments and buy a small unit near the MRT. Sean says the plan works, but decide what retirement means first.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should they sell the shop lot and cluster home, pay off the two apartments and buy a small unit in cash, or keep some properties for rent?
articles.answer: The plan is sound and would leave them debt-free with about RM3,300 a month in rent. But first decide what retirement means: stopping completely or slowing down. If they keep some income, there is no need to sell much, and with seven years to go they can sell gradually, when the market is good.
points: Stopping work changes the whole plan
Know what the money is for
Timing the sale can add value
Their daughters' homes are a good lesson

articles.title: Is buying a second property within a year too aggressive?
articles.excerpt: A 32-year-old working abroad wants a RM500,000 furnished Cheras subsale a year after buying her first unit, and worries falling birth rates will hurt property. Sean walks through the subsale steps and his long-term view.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is a second purchase this soon too aggressive, what happens in a subsale after she says yes, and will falling birth rates leave Malaysia with China-style oversupply?
articles.answer: Not too aggressive for her income and finances, and the building rents well. But as a member of a bulk-purchase club she should also weigh completed unsold units, which offer a subsale's certainty with a developer's discounts. Demographics will hurt outlying areas and big houses, not city units with job-driven demand.
points: A subsale takes about 18% in cash
One lawyer is cheaper and faster
Completed unsold units combine both
Fewer families means smaller city units

articles.title: Should I buy a second property, or keep it simple?
articles.excerpt: A 32-year-old government officer already owns a Klang Valley unit and invests in global equities. He asks whether two new projects with rebates are really good deals, or just sales tactics.
articles.viewerQuestion: Are these genuinely good investments or do the rebates make the numbers look better than they are, and with equities already in place, is another leveraged property worthwhile?
articles.answer: The rebates are retail-price sales tactics that everybody gets, and a newer project only wins when the entry price makes sense. Let the existing unit run, use your second 90% loan slot only when you can afford it, and keep the capital a third property would need in global equities.
points: Newer wins only if the price makes sense
Rebates are given to everybody
The exit depends on rent, not age
Cash in property is the worst deal
questions: Are property rebates and discounts from developers genuine savings or just sales tactics?
How do I know if a new launch is worth buying compared to an older unit?
What rental yield should I aim for so the rent covers my monthly instalment?
Should I buy a second property or put the money into global equities instead?
How much cash should I set aside for renovation and instalments before collecting my keys?

articles.title: How do we get the best price for the family home we must sell?
articles.excerpt: A 34-year-old plans to sell his overspending father's JB corner semi-D for RM2.2 million within two years to fund his parents' retirement. Sean explains how pricing, valuation and agents decide how fast it sells.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is two years long enough to sell at RM2.2 million, how does he get the best price, how does he pick an agent, and are there tax issues in the transfer?
articles.answer: Two years is plenty, and JB's market is strong, but price sets the speed. Get bank valuations first: asking well above what a bank will lend means buyers must find a large cash gap, so it will sit unsold. Pick one committed agent, and expect no RPGT on a home held this long.
points: Valuation decides what a buyer can borrow
Test the price, then lower it
One committed agent beats five
Protect the family first

articles.title: I own 10 fully paid condos at 59. Should I sell before I retire?
articles.excerpt: A viewer about to retire owns ten debt-free condos in Penang and Singapore. Sean agrees with selling the Penang units, but warns that selling too many too fast can be taxed as a business.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should KB sell some or all of the properties before retiring, move the money into fixed deposits and other assets, and stop dealing with tenants?
articles.answer: Selling the Penang units makes sense, perhaps keeping one, but slowly, so the sales aren't taxed as a property business. The three Singapore units are worth keeping for income.
points: Selling fast can be taxed as business
Singapore rent alone can fund retirement
Penang's LRT decides what to sell first
Refinancing is no longer the easy exit
questions: Should I sell my Penang condos before retiring?
How can I avoid being taxed as a business when selling multiple properties?
What is the RPGT rate for selling property in Malaysia?
Can rental income from Singapore properties fund retirement in Penang?
How does the Penang LRT affect property values and selling decisions?

articles.title: Should You Settle Your Housing Loan Early?
articles.excerpt: A reader with three mortgages dreams of being debt-free. Sean explains why he would keep the loans running, and what to do with the spare cash instead.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should she pay the loans off as fast as possible to save on interest, or let them run the full term?
articles.answer: Keep the loans running. At around 4%, a housing loan is the cheapest money you can get, below the rate of inflation, so spare cash should go where it earns more than the loan costs.
points: Settling early can raise your tax bill
Your cash can earn more elsewhere
Her loans already pay for themselves
Her age favours more borrowing, not less
questions: Should I pay off my housing loan early or keep it?
Is it better to invest spare cash or settle my mortgage?
How does rental income tax affect early loan settlement?
Can EPF dividends beat housing loan interest?
What buffer should I keep for rental properties?

articles.title: I work in Singapore. Can I get a housing loan in Malaysia?
articles.excerpt: Singapore income converts well, so qualifying is rarely the problem. Rena Choong explains what Malaysian banks check for Malaysians working in Singapore, and what changes if you take up citizenship.
articles.viewerQuestion: How do Malaysian banks treat Singapore income, and what should Malaysians working in Singapore prepare before applying?
articles.answer: Converted to ringgit, Singapore income usually qualifies easily; paperwork is what trips people up. Have at least a year of steady employment, clear savings records and your Singapore documents ready, and decide first whether you plan to settle there.
points: Income converts generously
Malaysians keep Malaysian margins
Citizenship changes the terms
Savings and history reassure the bank
questions: How do Malaysian banks assess income earned in Singapore for a housing loan?
What documents do I need to prepare for a Malaysian housing loan if I work in Singapore?
Does holding a Singapore PR affect my housing loan margin in Malaysia?
What happens to my Malaysian housing loan eligibility if I become a Singapore citizen?
Can I buy a property in Malaysia while owning an HDB flat in Singapore?

articles.title: Now settled in Singapore, what should I do with my new KL unit?
articles.excerpt: A young engineer bought a Bukit Jalil unit, then got Singapore PR. Sean explains why he would rent out the whole unit, how to furnish it for the right tenant, and why there is no rush to come home.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should he rent out the whole unit, rent it room by room and keep one room for visits, or let family stay, and how much should he spend getting it ready for tenants?
articles.answer: Rent out the whole unit and run it like a business, furnished for the tenants most likely to live there. Keeping a room for monthly visits or lending it to family wastes it, and there is no hurry to move back.
points: A spare room costs more than a hotel
The tenant decides the fit-out
Have more than one way to cover the loan
RM12,000 won't furnish a rental
questions: Should I rent out my whole unit or by room?
How much should I spend to furnish my rental unit?
What furniture do tenants look for?
Can I rent out my condo on Airbnb?
How does owning a Malaysian property affect Singapore PR?

articles.title: We own six properties that pay for themselves. Hold or start selling?
articles.excerpt: A couple in their 40s own a home and five rented units, all with positive cash flow. Sean explains how to decide whether to sell, hold or keep buying, starting with what the cash is for.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should they sell one property and keep the cash, and if so which one, or hold everything?
articles.answer: Decide what the money is for before selling anything. If they do sell, Sean would start with the small, low-yielding Shah Alam unit; otherwise they can hold, since every unit pays its way, and agree as a couple on how much is enough.
points: Their buffer is already solid
Cash loses value faster than it seems
Leasehold renewal has precedents
The smallest unit uses a full loan slot
questions: How do I decide whether to sell or hold my rental properties?
What should I do with the cash from selling an investment property?
How much cash buffer should I keep for my property portfolio?
Will my leasehold property lose value over time?
Should I sell my lowest-yielding property first?

articles.title: I lost my booking fee on a SOHO. Should I give up on property?
articles.excerpt: A young investor expected an 85% loan on a SOHO unit, got 70% and walked away from the booking. Sean explains the title mix-up and how he buys a third property and beyond.
articles.viewerQuestion: How should he book a subsale unit without risking the booking fee, how does Sean buy a third property and beyond, and is property even worth it when 30% upfront cash makes the returns worse than EPF?
articles.answer: Don't give up over a misunderstanding of the title: anything called SOHO is financed as a home, so a third one gets 70%. Beyond two properties, Sean buys through developer deals that need little cash, finances them on credit and keeps his own capital for stocks and other assets.
points: 'Home' in the name means a home loan
Subsale and auction need the most cash
Use credit for property, cash for the rest
Declared rent works for you
questions: How is a SOHO unit financed in Malaysia?
What is the loan margin for a third residential property?
How much cash is needed upfront for a subsale property?
Why are auctions risky for first-time buyers?
How can I buy a third property with little cash?

articles.title: Should I buy a Cheras condo on a staff loan before starting a family?
articles.excerpt: A 31-year-old who commutes three hours a day has booked a condo near an MRT station on a cheap staff loan. Sean's advice takes a turn: keep the cash and sort out the commute and family plans first.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is she doing the right thing for a first home bought to rent out now and live in later, should she look at subsale investments instead, and what else should she consider before starting a family?
articles.answer: Sean would hold off. The RM64,000 is worth more as a buffer while she starts a family, and the real problem, a three-hour daily commute, may be better solved by a job or a rental closer to home. If she does buy, it should be a pure investment that works on rent, which a subsale nearby may do better.
points: Mixed intentions need the 85% rule
The cash may be worth more than the cheap rate
With cash, a subsale may beat a new launch
A buffer buys choices
questions: Should I buy a condo to rent out first and live in later?
Is a staff loan worth using if it requires a large cash downpayment?
How do I compare a new launch condo with a subsale unit?
What should I consider before starting a family and buying a property?
Is a long commute a good reason to buy a property closer to work?

articles.title: My project has stalled. Will it be abandoned?
articles.excerpt: A buyer sees construction slowing and fears the project will be abandoned. Sean, a buyer in the same project, explains the difference between ailing and abandoned, and the real options for getting out or staying in.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is the project in trouble, and what can a buyer actually do if it ends up abandoned?
articles.answer: An ailing project is not an abandoned one. Check its official status, then choose between staying in for delay compensation or walking away at a cost. A full refund is very hard to get.
points: Ailing is not the same as abandoned
The developer is selling assets to fix it
Walking away costs money; a full refund is rare
Staying in can still pay off
questions: How do I check if my property project is officially ailing or abandoned?
What happens to my deposit if I cancel the sale and purchase agreement?
Can I get a full refund if my project is abandoned?
What compensation do I get if my property is delayed?
Should I continue paying my loan if the project is stalled?

articles.title: Is a student-rental unit near Sunway a good investment?
articles.excerpt: A 30-year-old is eyeing a USJ 1 project built for room-by-room student rentals, linked by BRT to the Sunway universities. Sean thinks it can work, but warns that only another investor will ever buy it from you.
articles.viewerQuestion: Are student investment properties around Sunway sound, what are the risks, does furnishing matter, and should he pay a company to manage the rooms?
articles.answer: It can work. Sunway's universities and schools aren't likely to move, which removes the biggest risk, and the agent's figures aren't unrealistic. The real risk is the exit: a unit built only for students can be sold only to investors, and only while its numbers still add up.
points: A campus moving out is the main risk
Only investors will buy it from you
Students wear buildings out
Furnishing is expected, and costs more

articles.title: I'm 20 and earn RM3,500. How should I prepare for property?
articles.excerpt: A 20-year-old accounting student running his own social media agency wants to start investing after graduating. Sean says to hold off and build the business first.
articles.viewerQuestion: What should he do over the next few years to prepare for his first property?
articles.answer: Don't make property the priority yet. While the business is young, flexibility and active income come first; property keeps you rich rather than makes you rich, so scale the agency and diversify once it earns well.
points: The business will out-earn any investment
Property ties up money
RM10,000 is not enough
Expecting fast money is the classic mistake

articles.title: I own two properties at 25. How do I reach RM10 million?
articles.excerpt: A 25-year-old second-generation business owner holds two KL properties bought below market and wants RM10 million in property within ten years. Sean says to pause and grow elsewhere.
articles.viewerQuestion: How should he grow towards RM10 million in property in ten years: commercial property, a purchase using his wife's foreigner quota, or more residential?
articles.answer: For now, don't grow it. He already has the two or three properties Sean encourages over a lifetime, so the next step is to settle the second unit, put his own money into other, uncorrelated assets, and grow his income and business knowledge, because property keeps you rich rather than makes you rich.
points: A third property is expensive
Commercial property is playing with fire
Diversify into uncorrelated assets
Judge success by cash flow, not asset value

articles.title: My tenant has stopped paying rent. What can I legally do?
articles.excerpt: A tenant who stops paying but won't leave is every landlord's nightmare. Lawyer Tea explains the legal route Sean's viewers can take: a letter of demand, then a court distress order.
articles.viewerQuestion: When a tenant stops paying rent and won't leave, what is the legal way to get your money and your property back?
articles.answer: Act on the first missed month: send a letter of demand, and if the tenant hasn't paid within 14 days, apply to court for a distress order. The order lets you seize and auction the tenant's belongings and take the unit back, in two to three months at best.
points: Start while the deposit still covers you
A distress order moves quickly
Doing it yourself can backfire
Paperwork decides what you recover
questions: What is the legal process to evict a tenant who hasn't paid rent?
How long does a distress order take to recover possession?
Can I cut off utilities or change locks if my tenant stops paying?
What documents do I need to prove a tenancy in court?
How much does it cost to get a letter of demand and distress order?

articles.title: Should my third property be subsale, auction, new or bulk purchase?
articles.excerpt: A 30-year-old with two landed homes and RM200,000 to RM300,000 in cash weighs subsale, auction, new and bulk purchase for her third. Sean says to keep her cash and let the deal decide.
articles.viewerQuestion: For her third property, should she use cash on a subsale or auction unit with 10% down, or buy new or through bulk purchase, and save her cash?
articles.answer: Keep the cash and use credit. Sean has no favourite channel; he buys wherever the best deal is, but with her aim of letting the property pay for itself, new launches and bulk purchases fit better than subsale or auction, and her savings are worth more as runway for her business.
points: Less cash in means more options later
A bigger discount beats a standard one
Auctions carry hidden problems
Her business may out-earn her job

articles.title: Unsold units near completion: warning sign or better deal?
articles.excerpt: A first-time investor sees plenty of units still for sale in a project close to handover. Sean explains why developers end up with unsold stock, and when that works in a buyer's favour.
articles.viewerQuestion: Do the unsold units signal a problem, does the delay matter to a buyer like him, and are dual-key and tri-key units worth it?
articles.answer: Not in this case. Few Malaysians can borrow for a unit above RM1 million, so slow sales near completion are expected, and a developer that keeps building through a delay is a financially strong one. Judge the unit on location, rent and long-term value, and treat any discount as a bonus.
points: Developers clear stock quietly
Price limits who can buy
Delay hurts families more than investors
Dual-key units stretch one loan slot
questions: Do unsold units near completion mean the project is in trouble?
Are dual-key or tri-key units worth buying?
Does a late delivery matter if I buy close to completion?
How do I compare expected rent with my instalment?
Should I buy a completed unsold unit instead of one under construction?

articles.title: How do I know a location suits me before buying a home?
articles.excerpt: Viewers often ask Sean whether a home is worth buying. He can't know their lives, so he offers two tests to run first: affordability, then a weekday and a weekend in the new location.
articles.viewerQuestion: How can you tell whether a home and its location will suit your life before you commit?
articles.answer: Run two tests. First, can you carry the instalment for 30 to 35 years? Only then picture an ordinary weekday and weekend from that address, from the commute to school runs and errands, and see whether it still works.
points: The instalment shapes your whole life
Weekdays are most of your life
Don't buy for a once-a-month view
Bigger isn't always better

articles.title: Is it a good time to buy? What ten years of data says
articles.excerpt: Why did some Malaysians lose money on property over the past decade? Sean reads ten years of official data and swaps timing for a test you can actually apply.
articles.viewerQuestion: Why did some buyers lose money over the last decade, and how do you tell whether it is a good time to buy?
articles.answer: Nobody can time the market, so stop trying. If your finances are ready, buy only below the location's past transacted median, with rent that gives a healthy yield. That limits the damage even if you happen to buy at a peak.
points: When you bought decided who lost
Property does not double every ten years
Nobody can call the bottom
The outlook is positive, but supply is rising
questions: Why did some people lose money buying property in Malaysia over the past ten years?
Is now a good time to buy property in Malaysia?
How much do house prices actually rise in Malaysia each year?
What rental yield should I look for before buying a property?
Should I buy below the median transacted price in an area?

articles.title: What happens to my properties when I die?
articles.excerpt: Property owners spend decades building a portfolio but rarely plan how it passes on. Two succession lawyers explain what happens with and without a will, and how to prepare one.
articles.viewerQuestion: What happens to your properties if you die, with or without a will, and how should a property owner prepare?
articles.answer: Without a will, the Distribution Act decides who inherits, and your family must go to court before anyone can act. A will lets you name an executor and decide who gets what, and the lawyers treat it as a plan for your family, not just a list of assets.
points: Without a will, the law picks your heirs
Your family needs a court order first
Loans don't fall due at once
Executors must trace assets and debts first
questions: What happens to my properties if I die without a will?
How do I prepare a will for my property in Malaysia?
Who inherits my house if I pass away without a will?
What does an executor do when distributing properties?
How are outstanding housing loans handled when the owner dies?
